steps: Spot the pivot and which distance is perpendicular to the force
If given a mass, find its weight with W = mg first
Balanced beam or lever: set clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment
Gears: ratio = driven teeth ÷ driver teeth (speed divides, force multiplies)
method_card.title: Moments, Levers and Gears
method_card.content:
A moment is the turning effect of a force: M = F × d, where d is the perpendicular distance from the pivot, in metres.

  • Rearrange for a missing value: F = M ÷ d, or d = M ÷ F.
  • Given a mass? Find its weight first: W = m × g (g = 9.8 N/kg).
  • Balanced beam or lever: clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment, so F₁d₁ = F₂d₂.
  • Several forces on one side: add their moments before balancing.
  • A uniform beam's weight acts at its centre.
  • Gears: ratio = driven teeth ÷ driver teeth; speed ÷ ratio, force × ratio.

gold.display: Diagram not drawn accuratelyA beam is balanced on a pivot. On the left side: a 100 N force acts 0.5 m from the pivot, and a 200 N force acts 1.5 m from the pivot. What single force on the right, at 0.7 m from the pivot, is needed to balance the beam?

misconceptions.message: With multiple forces on one side, calculate each moment separately then add: (100 × 0.5) + (200 × 1.5) = 350 Nm.

guided_steps.say: Multiple forces on the left: work out each moment, add them, then balance against the right.
So F = 500 N.

guided_steps.done: It equals the 350 Nm total, so 500 N balances the beam.

gold.hint: Add both left moments, then divide the total by the right-hand distance.

gold.display: A gear system has a driver gear with 20 teeth and a driven gear with 60 teeth. The driver gear rotates at 120 rpm. Calculate the speed of the driven gear in rpm.

misconceptions.message: Gear ratio = 60/20 = 3. The driven gear turns 3× slower: 120 ÷ 3 = 40 rpm.
A larger driven gear turns SLOWER. Divide the speed by the gear ratio, don't multiply.

guided_steps.say: Gears: work out the gear ratio = driven teeth ÷ driver teeth. A bigger driven gear turns slower.

guided_steps.hint: Divide driven teeth by driver teeth.

guided_steps.pre: The driven gear turns 3 times slower, so divide the speed: 120 ÷ 3 =
guided_steps.hint: Divide the input speed by the gear ratio.
guided_steps.say: So the driven gear turns at 40 rpm.

guided_steps.done: It returns the driver's 120 rpm, so 40 rpm is right.

gold.hint: Gear ratio = driven ÷ driver; a bigger driven gear turns slower, so divide the speed.

gold.display: A gear system has a driver gear with 20 teeth and a driven gear with 60 teeth. If the input force is 15 N, calculate the output force (assuming no energy losses).

misconceptions.message: Gear ratio = 60/20 = 3. The driven gear has 3× more force: 15 × 3 = 45 N. Larger gear = more force.
A larger driven gear multiplies force. Multiply by the gear ratio, not divide.

guided_steps.say: Same gear ratio, but force behaves the opposite way to speed: a bigger driven gear gives MORE force.

guided_steps.hint: Divide driven teeth by driver teeth.
Multiply the input force by the gear ratio.
guided_steps.say: So the output force is 45 N.

guided_steps.done: It returns the 15 N input, so 45 N is right.

gold.hint: Gear ratio = driven ÷ driver; a bigger driven gear gives more force, so multiply.

gold.display: Diagram not drawn accuratelyA uniform beam is 2.0 m long with mass 10 kg. The pivot is 0.8 m from the left end. A 50 N load hangs from the left end. Calculate the force needed at the right end to balance the beam. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: Beam weight = 10 × 9.8 = 98 N at centre (1.0 m from left = 0.2 m right of pivot). ACW = 50 × 0.8 = 40 Nm. CW = 98 × 0.2 = 19.6 Nm + F × 1.2. So 40 = 19.6 + 1.2F. F = 20.4/1.2 = 17 N.
A uniform beam's weight acts at its centre. The centre is 1.0 m from the left end.

guided_steps.say: A uniform beam's own weight acts at its centre. Find that weight and where it acts, then balance.

guided_steps.pre: The centre is 1.0 m from the left; the pivot is at 0.8 m, so the weight acts 1.0 − 0.8 =
Anticlockwise moment from the 50 N load, 0.8 m left of the pivot: 50 × 0.8 =
guided_steps.hint: Load times its distance from the pivot.

guided_steps.pre: Clockwise moment from the beam weight: 98 × 0.2 =
guided_steps.hint: Weight times its distance right of the pivot.

guided_steps.pre: The right force acts 2.0 − 0.8 = 1.2 m from the pivot. Balance gives 40 = 19.6 + F × 1.2. First, 40 − 19.6 =
guided_steps.hint: Subtract the beam's moment from the load's moment.

guided_steps.say: So F = 17 N.

guided_steps.done: It equals the 40 Nm anticlockwise moment, so 17 N balances.

gold.hint: Find the beam's weight and where its centre acts, then balance the moments about the pivot.

gold.display: A lever is connected to an input gear with 15 teeth. A force of 12 N is applied 0.3 m from the pivot on the lever. The output gear has 45 teeth. Calculate the output torque (moment) from the gear system in Nm.

misconceptions.message: Input torque = 12 × 0.3 = 3.6 Nm. Gear ratio = 45/15 = 3. Output torque = 3.6 × 3 = 10.8 Nm.
More teeth on output = more torque. Multiply the input torque by the gear ratio.

guided_steps.say: Two steps: first the lever's moment (torque), then multiply by the gear ratio.

guided_steps.hint: Multiply the lever torque by the gear ratio.
guided_steps.say: So the output torque is 10.8 Nm.

guided_steps.done: It returns the 3.6 Nm lever torque, so 10.8 Nm is right.

gold.hint: Work out the lever's torque first, then multiply by the gear ratio.

gold.display: A crowbar is used to lift a heavy stone. The effort of 80 N is applied 0.75 m from the pivot. The stone rests 0.05 m from the pivot. Calculate the maximum force exerted on the stone.

misconceptions.message: Effort × effort distance = load × load distance. 80 × 0.75 = F × 0.05. F = 60 ÷ 0.05 = 1200 N.
The load is closer to the pivot, so the force is multiplied. Mechanical advantage = 0.75/0.05 = 15.

guided_steps.say: A lever multiplies force: effort × effort distance = load × load distance.

guided_steps.hint: Effort force times its distance from the pivot.
Divide by the load's distance from the pivot.
guided_steps.say: So the force on the stone is 1200 N.

guided_steps.done: It equals the 60 Nm effort moment, so 1200 N is right.

gold.hint: Effort × effort distance = load × load distance; rearrange for the load force.

misconceptions.message: Moment = force × distance = 50 × 0.3 = 15 Nm.

guided_steps.say: Moments use one equation: M = F × d, the force times the perpendicular distance from the pivot.

guided_steps.hint: It is given as the perpendicular distance in the question.
Multiply the force by the distance.
guided_steps.say: So M = 15 Nm.

guided_steps.hint: Divide the moment by the force.
guided_steps.done: It returns 0.3 m, the distance, so 15 Nm is right.

bronze.hint: Multiply the force by the perpendicular distance.

bronze.display: A moment of 20 Nm is produced by a force acting 0.4 m from a pivot. Calculate the force.

guided_steps.hint: In F = M ÷ d the moment is divided by the distance.
Divide the moment by the distance.
guided_steps.say: So F = 50 N.

guided_steps.done: It returns the 20 Nm moment, so 50 N is right.

bronze.hint: Rearrange to F = M ÷ d, then divide.

guided_steps.say: M = F × d. You want the distance, so rearrange: d = M ÷ F.

guided_steps.pre: The moment goes on top. M =

Divide the moment by the force.

bronze.display: Diagram not drawn accuratelyA seesaw is balanced. A 400 N force acts 2.0 m from the pivot on the left. A force acts 1.6 m from the pivot on the right. What is the force on the right?

guided_steps.say: A balanced seesaw: clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment, so F₁d₁ = F₂d₂.

guided_steps.pre: Work out the known moment first: 400 × 2.0 =
guided_steps.hint: Force times distance on the left.

guided_steps.pre: This equals F × 1.6. Divide to find F: 800 ÷ 1.6 =
guided_steps.hint: Divide the moment by the right-hand distance.
guided_steps.say: So F = 500 N.

guided_steps.hint: Force times distance on the right.
guided_steps.done: It matches the left moment of 800 Nm, so 500 N balances.

bronze.hint: Balance the moments: F₁d₁ = F₂d₂, then rearrange for the unknown force.

silver.display: A child of mass 30 kg sits 2.0 m from the pivot of a seesaw. An adult of mass 60 kg sits on the other side. How far from the pivot must the adult sit to balance? (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: First find weights: child = 30 × 9.8 = 294 N, adult = 60 × 9.8 = 588 N. Then 294 × 2 = 588 × d. d = 588/588 = 1.0 m.
Use weight (W = mg), not mass, in the moment equation.

guided_steps.say: First turn the masses into weights with W = mg (g = 9.8), then balance: W₁d₁ = W₂d₂.

guided_steps.hint: Divide the child's moment by the adult's weight.
guided_steps.say: So d = 1.0 m.

guided_steps.done: It equals the child's 588 Nm moment, so 1.0 m balances.

silver.hint: Turn both masses into weights with W = mg, then balance the moments.

silver.display: Diagram not drawn accuratelyA 600 N force acts 0.8 m from a pivot (clockwise). What force at 1.2 m from the pivot (anticlockwise) is needed to balance it?

guided_steps.say: Balance: clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment.
So F = 400 N.

guided_steps.done: It matches the 480 Nm clockwise moment, so 400 N balances.

silver.hint: Set the clockwise moment equal to the anticlockwise one, then divide.

silver.display: A nutcracker has the nut 0.08 m from the pivot and the handle 0.4 m from the pivot. A 5 kg mass is placed in the nutcracker. Calculate the force you need to apply at the handle to crack it. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: Convert mass to weight first: W = mg = 5 × 9.8 = 49 N.

guided_steps.say: First turn the mass into a weight (W = mg), then balance the load and effort moments.

guided_steps.hint: Weight times the nut's distance from the pivot.

guided_steps.say: So you apply 9.8 N at the handle.

guided_steps.done: It equals the 3.92 Nm load moment, so 9.8 N is right.

silver.hint: Turn the mass into a weight first, then balance the load and effort moments.

silver.display: Diagram not drawn accuratelyA beam has a pivot in the centre. A 200 N force acts 1.0 m to the left of the pivot. A 150 N force acts 2.0 m to the right. Calculate the resultant moment. State the direction (clockwise or anticlockwise). Give your answer as the magnitude only.

misconceptions.message: ACW moment = 200 × 1 = 200 Nm. CW moment = 150 × 2 = 300 Nm. Resultant = 300 − 200 = 100 Nm clockwise.

guided_steps.say: Work out each moment, then subtract, because the two forces turn opposite ways.

guided_steps.pre: They oppose, so subtract the smaller from the larger: 300 − 200 =
guided_steps.hint: Subtract the anticlockwise moment from the clockwise one.
guided_steps.say: So the resultant is 100 Nm, clockwise.

guided_steps.hint: Add the resultant back to the anticlockwise moment.
guided_steps.done: It equals the 300 Nm clockwise moment, so 100 Nm is right.

silver.hint: Find each moment, then subtract because they turn opposite ways.

silver.display: An 8 kg mass hangs from a horizontal bar at a distance of 0.25 m from the pivot. Calculate the moment about the pivot. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

misconceptions.message: First find weight: W = 8 × 9.8 = 78.4 N. Moment = 78.4 × 0.25 = 19.6 Nm.

guided_steps.say: Turn the mass into a weight (W = mg), then take the moment.
So the moment is 19.6 Nm.

guided_steps.hint: Divide the moment by the distance.
guided_steps.done: It returns the 78.4 N weight, so 19.6 Nm is right.

silver.hint: Turn the mass into a weight with W = mg, then multiply by the distance.

silver.display: A wheelbarrow has its load of 150 N at 0.4 m from the wheel (pivot). The handles are 1.2 m from the wheel. Calculate the effort needed at the handles to lift the load.

misconceptions.message: Load × load distance = effort × effort distance. 150 × 0.4 = F × 1.2. F = 60 ÷ 1.2 = 50 N.

guided_steps.say: A wheelbarrow is a lever: load × load distance = effort × effort distance.

guided_steps.hint: Load times its distance from the wheel.

guided_steps.say: So the effort needed is 50 N.

guided_steps.done: It equals the 60 Nm load moment, so 50 N lifts it.

silver.hint: Balance the load moment against the effort moment, then divide.

problem_bank.gold_description: Chain two steps: add several moments, run a gear ratio, or include a uniform beam's own weight.
